newsitem.title: USA: "Jenny Jones" producer testifies at murder trial.
newsitem.headline: "Jenny Jones" producer testifies at murder trial.

text.p: A "Jenny Jones Show" producer testified on Friday that she told murder suspect Jonathan Schmitz the person who would reveal a secret crush on him before a national TV audience could have been either a man or a woman.

Schmitz, 26, is charged with the shotgun murder of Scott Amedure three days after the two appeared in a taping of a "Jenny Jones" segment on same-sex secret crushes in March 1995. During the show, Amedure revealed his affection for Schmitz, who says he is heterosexual.
Karen Lautens-Campbell, the producer who handled the same-sex crush show, testified on Friday that "surprise" was a key element of the show's topic.

She said she phoned Schmitz to persuade him to be a guest on the show but admittedly told him it was about "secret admirers," even though it really was about same-sex crushes. She added that she did not see a difference between the two.
"I told him it could be a man or a woman. It was his choice to come on the show," Lautens-Campbell said.
Oakland County Circuit Judge Francis O'Brien was expected to rule next week whether talk show host Jenny Jones will have to testify in the trial.

The issue of deception is central to the defence of Schmitz, who says the humiliation he suffered on the nationally syndicated TV talk show, coupled with mental illnesses he suffers from, drove him to shoot Amedure twice in the chest at Amedure's Orion Township, Michigan mobile home.

Donna Riley, a mutual friend of Amedure and Schmitz, had contacted the show to suggest that the two appear together after seeing a televised advertisement seeking guests who wanted to reveal crushes on persons of the same sex.

Schmitz' defence attorney, James Burdick, pressed Lautens-Campbell to admit that she lied to Schmitz, but she refused. "She doesn't call it a lie, but it's obviously a lie," Burdick told reporters outside the courtroom.

Lautens-Campbell, who left the show in May 1996 to start her own television production firm with two other former "Jenny Jones" employees, including her husband, did admit that Schmitz was worried about his "secret admirer" being a man.
In notes she made from their telephone conversation, she wrote that Schmitz told her, "I don't want a guy saying this to me on the air."

Lautens-Campbell also testified that she wrote in a memorandum to Jenny Jones that she thought Schmitz would be shocked by Amedure's affection for him. "I think Jon is going to die when he sees it's Scott," she wrote.

In another document, written up from pre-show interviews with Amedure, Schmitz and Riley, Lautens-Campbell said she wrote about Amedure: "He's always talking about how hot Jon's body is and how he wants to rip him apart."
But Lautens-Campbell said she considers Amedure's murder unrelated to the show. "Everyone came on by their own choice to have fun," she said.

Last week a tape of the programme, which never aired, was shown in court, including a segment in which Schmitz finds out that Amedure was his secret admirer and laughs while burying his face in his hands.
